findings.paper_title: September 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet - Final
findings.headline: Early payment of £3.052m Transport for City Regions highway maintenance grant is drawn down into 2026/27 from the future allocation.
findings.detail: The paper says this changes the timing of the funding rather than the total allocation. The remaining TCR allocation is reprofiled across 2027/28 to 2031/32, and the early payment is to be considered by SYMCA's Board on 27 October 2026. The grant will be applied to existing highway maintenance projects, allowing corporate borrowing to be carried forward.
findings.matters: Drawing future grant forward and using it to defer corporate borrowing is a timing lever peers in South Yorkshire and elsewhere may use, and it moves funding out of later years.
findings.figures: £3.052m early TCR drawdown in 2026/27; £34.629m total TCR Highway Capital Maintenance allocation; 30.52% Rotherham share; around £5.9m per year 2027/28 to 2029/30; £6.9m per year 2030/31 to 2031/32

findings.paper_title: September 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet - Final
findings.headline: General Fund unsupported borrowing in the funded capital programme totals £162.940m across 2026/27 to 2029/30.

The paper says the council will need to closely consider the level of prudential borrowing to keep overall debt manageable and guard against interest rate risk.
findings.matters: Unsupported borrowing of this scale against a rising DSG deficit and a mid-year overspend is the figure lenders and finance directors will use to judge the council's future debt-servicing headroom.
findings.quote: The Council will need to closely consider the level of prudential borrowing

findings.paper_title: Final - July 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet
findings.headline: Property and Facilities Services forecast £1.0m overspend (up £0.7m since May), with Facilities Management overspend of £1.2m on repairs and maintenance
findings.detail: Property and Facilities Services is now forecasting £1.0m overspend, a significant worsening of £0.7m since May. Facilities Management alone accounts for £1.2m overspend driven by 'assorted building costs, largely repairs and maintenance,' up £0.2m since the last report. Catering is now £0.3m overspent (previously balanced) due to lower-than-expected income, though Cleaning Services underspend of £0.7m partially offsets this.
findings.matters: Maintenance and repairs backlogs are structural and typically grow rather than shrink; this is a signal of asset condition issues. The worsening trend (£0.7m deterioration in two months) suggests the council may face increasing capital maintenance pressures.
findings.figures: £1.0m total PFS overspend (up £0.7m); Facilities Management £1.2m overspend (up £0.2m); Catering £0.3m overspend (previously balanced)

findings.paper_title: Final - July 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital Programme expanded by £25.8m (from £180.7m to £206.5m) with heavy reliance on unsupported borrowing (£162.8m of £284.3m General Fund = 57% over four years)
findings.detail: The capital programme has been expanded significantly: General Fund capital increased to £120.9m for 2026/27 (from £109.7m originally), with total four-year programme of £284.3m. The funding mix shows heavy reliance on unsupported borrowing: £162.8m of £284.3m (57%) is via prudential borrowing, with grants and contributions only £120.8m. The report notes the council 'will need to keep close control of project spend profiles' and 'potentially, re-profile some schemes into future financial years.' Interest rate and refinancing risk is flagged.
findings.matters: A capital programme 57%-funded by borrowing, in a council already running a £5.9m operating deficit, increases financial risk materially. The acknowledgement that re-profiling may be needed suggests deliverability risk. Interest rate movements will directly impact the council's debt service capacity.
findings.figures: £206.5m total capital (up from £180.7m); £120.9m General Fund; £162.8m of £284.3m (four-year) funded by unsupported borrowing (57%); HRA £85.6m also includes £84.95m borrowing
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026/27 remains ambitious even with a significant level of re-profiling of schemes into 2027/28. The Council will therefore need to keep close control of project spend profiles and delivery milestones to keep these projects on track. The Council will also need to review the deliverability of this increased Capital Programme and potentially, re-profile some schemes into future financial years.

findings.paper_title: Final - July 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet
findings.headline: Legal Services overspend of £0.4m driven by ongoing recruitment challenges and reliance on external locums and counsel, with new pressures from Supreme Court ruling on Deprivation of Liberty
findings.detail: Legal Services is forecasting a £0.4m overspend due to persistent recruitment difficulties and reliance on locums and external suppliers. Additional pressures include a Supreme Court ruling that 'has significantly changed the approach to Deprivation of Liberty applications,' costs from ongoing litigation, and support for the National Grooming Gang Inquiry. The report notes this reflects 'a wider local government workforce issue.' Permanent recruitment campaigns have been unsuccessful.
findings.matters: This indicates structural staffing challenges that cannot be easily fixed; the council is paying premium costs for external labour to cover what should be permanent roles. The new legal obligations from the Supreme Court ruling create an unfunded cost pressure.
findings.figures: £0.4m overspend (£0.1m from CYPS, £0.2m from Adult Social Care); locum and external counsel reliance due to unfilled permanent posts
findings.quote: recruitment to permanent legal posts remains challenging despite ongoing campaigns, reflecting a wider local government workforce issue. As a result, the service continues to rely on locums and external providers, including King's Counsel where necessary, to maintain capacity and meet statutory and operational requirements.

findings.paper_title: Final - July 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet
findings.headline: Home to School Transport overspend of £1.1m (previously reported as balanced), with forecast uncertain pending confirmation of September 2026 cohort
findings.detail: Home to School Transport shifted from a previously balanced position to a £1.1m overspend forecast. The council acknowledges this forecast 'assumes that all children using the service at the end of the academic year will continue to do so in September, so further changes are possible once the 2026/27 cohort is known.' Detailed work is underway to quantify the drivers. This is a material shift in forecast with acknowledged uncertainty.
findings.matters: A £1.1m swing in forecast on a demand-driven service signals either a significant underestimate in the original budget or rapid demand growth. The acknowledged uncertainty ('further changes are possible') means this forecast may still move.
findings.figures: £1.1m overspend; previously reported as balanced (as of June 2026); subject to change pending September cohort confirmation
findings.quote: Home to School Transport is forecasting a £1.1m overspend, which was previously reported as balanced. This position assumes that all children using the service at the end of the academic year will continue to do so in September, so further changes are possible once the 2026/27 cohort is known.

findings.paper_title: Final - July 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet
findings.headline: Waste service operating with hire vehicles, forecast £1.5m overspend worsened by £0.9m since May, waiting for new council-owned vehicles to arrive
findings.detail: The Waste service is forecasting a £1.5m overspend (up from £0.6m in May, a £0.9m deterioration), primarily driven by transport overspends. The root cause is the service is 'operating with a high number of hire and spare vehicles' while new council-owned vehicles (which are more cost-effective) are awaited. A route optimisation programme to remove two routes has not yet been delivered due to difficulties in autumn 2025/26. The report expects improvement only when new vehicles arrive in March 2026 (though this appears to be a forward reference within a July 2026 report, suggesting vehicles may not have arrived as planned).
findings.matters: This is an operational inefficiency causing material cost overrun; the council is paying premium hire costs while waiting for capital investment. The deterioration of £0.9m in two months and the stated delay in route optimisation suggest the council has limited near-term control over this cost.
findings.figures: £1.5m overspend; worsened by £0.9m since May; route optimisation saving (part of £1.040m R&E savings target) not yet delivered
findings.quote: The Waste service is forecasting to be £1.5m overspent, which is a worsening of £0.9m. This is largely caused by overspends on transport, as the service continues to operate with a high number of hire and spare vehicles, required as the new Council owned, more cost effective vehicles, will not arrive until March 2026 and the route optimisation programme has yet to be delivered in full.

findings.paper_title: Final - July 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet
findings.headline: Savings plan significantly underdelivered: £3.633m target, only £2.413m secured; £1.220m still to be delivered (66% delivery rate)
findings.detail: The council approved £3.633m of savings for 2026/27, but has only secured £2.413m (66%) by end of July. This leaves £1.220m undelivered: £900k in Adult Care (Working Age Adults), £320k in Regeneration (Waste Route Optimisation), and £40k in Property Services. The report states 'activity is ongoing' but provides no timeline or confidence in delivery.
findings.matters: Undelivered savings have a direct impact on the forecast outturn; if the remaining £1.220m is not delivered, the overspend will widen from £5.9m to £7.1m. Historically weak delivery on savings (prior year had £440k undelivered) suggests this is a structural issue, not a timing one.
findings.figures: £3.633m target; £2.413m secured; £1.220m still to deliver (66% delivery rate); £900k Adult Care, £320k Waste, £40k Property
findings.quote: Currently, £2.413m of delivery has been secured... Activity is ongoing to deliver the remaining £1.220m of savings that relate to Working Age Adults £0.900m, Waste Route Optimisation £0.280m and Waleswood £0.040m.

findings.paper_title: Final - July 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet
findings.headline: DSG in-year deficit £6.4m; cumulative deficit projected £19.9m by March 2028 when override ends
findings.detail: Rotherham is forecasting a £6.4m in-year DSG deficit (primarily High Needs Block), deteriorating by £0.9m in two months. The cumulative deficit is forecast to hit £9.3m by end 2026/27 and reach £19.9m by March 2028 when the government's statutory override ends. The council expects government support via the High Needs Stability Grant (covering 90% of eligible deficits to 31 March 2026) but with assumptions subject to DfE policy decisions; without government support, the council would need to absorb the deficit into its General Fund.
findings.matters: A £19.9m cumulative deficit is a material liability that becomes a direct charge to the General Fund once statutory protection ends in March 2028. If government support is withdrawn or insufficient, it represents an existential budget pressure that cannot be deferred. This is a major tail risk for lenders.
findings.figures: £6.4m in-year deficit (up from £5.5m in May); cumulative deficit £9.3m by end 2026/27; projected £19.9m by March 2028; High Needs Stability Grant covers 90% of deficits to 31 March 2026 only
findings.quote: The Council is forecasting an in-year DSG deficit of £6.4m, primarily within the High Needs Block, representing a £0.9m deterioration since May... The Council's DSG cumulative deficit is projected to reach £19.9m by March 2028 when the statutory protection ends and could increase by around £10m per year thereafter if current demand and inflationary pressures continue.

findings.paper_title: Final - July 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet
findings.headline: Children in Care placements £6.0m overspent, with 48 children in external residential homes against a budget for 40, and an increasing proportion in high-cost placements at £10,000+ per week
findings.detail: CYPS forecasts a £6.0m overspend on Children in Care placements, slightly better than May (£6.2m) but still the largest single budget pressure in the council. The number of children in external residential has grown to 48 (vs 40 budgeted), with a particular issue being children placed in high-cost residential due to complexity of needs. Occupancy at council-owned homes has fallen to 76%, down from 82%, suggesting placement mix constraints.
findings.matters: Social care placement inflation is a key risk factor for council solvency; structural demand/cost increases that outpace budget assume the council will eventually have to either cut spending (difficult for statutory services) or draw reserves. This is the largest single budget pressure.
findings.figures: £6.0m overspend; 48 external residential placements vs 40 budgeted; 8 children in high-cost residential (£10,000/week); 76% occupancy in council homes (down from 82%)
findings.quote: External residential placements remain the main driver of the placement budget pressures, with 48 children placed in external children's homes in July against a budgeted profile of 40. This pressure is further compounded by the increasing number of children placed in high-cost residential provision (at a weekly cost of £10,000 and above) due to the complexity of their needs.

findings.paper_title: Final - July 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet
findings.headline: Revenue budget overspend of £5.9m, driven by £10.9m directorate overspends only partially offset by central services savings

The council states it 'will need to put in place actions to mitigate the projected overspend position' but 'cannot forecast that improvement until clear actions have been identified.'
findings.matters: An unmitigated overspend of this size signals both immediate cash pressure and potential reserve depletion, which directly affects a lender's view of financial resilience and the council's ability to service debt.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report Q1 2026-27
findings.headline: Discounted PWLB rate for HRA long-term borrowing expires in March 2027
findings.detail: The council has access to a preferential PWLB interest rate specifically for HRA debt, but this facility closes in March 2027 (eight months away). The council notes it may use this rate for some long-term borrowing 'depending on the prevailing interest rate position' but has not yet committed to doing so.
findings.matters: This is a time-limited window to lock in more favourable long-term borrowing costs for housing. The council needs to decide soon whether to use it, as delay will mean refinancing at standard (higher) rates.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report Q1 2026-27
findings.headline: HRA financing costs ratio has risen from 13.47% to 13.89% in Q1
findings.detail: The proportion of Housing Revenue Account spending devoted to debt financing costs has increased by 0.42 percentage points in the first quarter. The council attributes this to in-year capital programme changes and interest rate movements. This leaves less room in the HRA for maintenance, improvement, or rent restraint.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs as a share of HRA revenue compress the council's flexibility in the housing business. A sustained upward trend would put pressure on HRA balances or require either higher rents or deferred maintenance.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs ratio: 13.47% to 13.89%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report Q1 2026-27
findings.headline: Interest rate outlook has deteriorated while the council's strategy depends on rates falling
findings.detail: Rotherham has relied on short-term borrowing to generate savings that have been 'essential to achieving balanced budgets'. However, PWLB rates are now at their highest levels for a number of years (50-year rate at 6.35%), six-month borrowing rates have risen from 4.2% to 4.4%, and the council now faces 'increased uncertainty around the future direction of interest rates' due to geopolitical events. If rates remain elevated rather than falling as the strategy assumes, the savings that have underpinned budget balance are at risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether Rotherham's budget assumptions rest on interest rate forecasts that may not materialize. The council's financial resilience depends partly on savings from this strategy, so a sustained rate environment higher than expected would create pressure.
findings.figures: PWLB 50-year rate 6.35% (highest in years), six-month borrowing rates 4.4% (up from 4.2% June 2025), £50m temporary borrowing refinanced
findings.quote: the future outlook is more challenging. There is increased uncertainty around the future direction of interest rates as markets respond to the recent conflict in Iran.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Summary of Prudential Indicators for Rotherham MBC
findings.headline: Under-borrowing (excluding PFI) increased to £209.887m from an original forecast of £29.456m, a seven-fold expansion in the gap between Capital Financing Requirement and actual borrowing.
findings.detail: The council's under-borrowing position — the gap between its financing need and actual borrowing — has grown substantially from the original forecast. While revised estimates predicted £211.326m under-borrowing, the original budget had forecast only £29.456m. This shift partly reflects the capital programme underspend, but indicates the council's actual debt position differs materially from initial estimates.
findings.matters: Material divergence between estimated and actual borrowing signals either unexecuted capital investment or revised funding strategies; this affects lenders' assessment of the council's debt capacity and future refinancing needs.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Summary of Prudential Indicators for Rotherham MBC
findings.headline: Non-HRA financing costs ratio rose to 12.24%, exceeding both the revised estimate of 10.11% and the original estimate of 11.52%.
findings.detail: The actual ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream for non-HRA services reached 12.24%, above both revised (10.11%) and original (11.52%) estimates. The HRA ratio also increased to 15.06% against a revised estimate of 14.15%. These ratios indicate what share of the council's revenue must service debt, and both came in worse than forecast.
findings.matters: Higher financing costs reduce funds available for service delivery; lenders and peers monitor this ratio as a measure of financial sustainability and the burden of debt relative to available revenue.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure came in at £150.613m, 30% below the revised estimate of £214.194m and 38% below the original budget of £241.993m.
findings.detail: The council's actual capital spending was £150.613m against a revised estimate of £214.194m. This underspend of £63.581m suggests either delayed projects, reduced investment plans, or slowed delivery. The gap between revised and original estimates (£214.194m vs £241.993m) had already flagged reduced capital expectations.
findings.matters: Capital delivery is a key measure of council performance and financial management; significant underspending may indicate delivery challenges or revised capital priorities that affect future borrowing needs and the council's ability to execute its infrastructure plans.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council is pursuing short-term borrowing strategy with acknowledged refinancing risk in the near term
findings.detail: Rotherham has increased short-term borrowing to £137.241m (up from £110.232m), comprising £60.241m PWLB and £77m market loans. The report explicitly states this strategy will result in 'an increased refinancing risk in the near term.' The council is betting that when these loans mature in 12-24 months, refinancing rates will be lower than the 3.89%-4.65% it is currently paying.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand refinancing concentration risk. The council has £137m of debt maturing in the next two years, and if rates do not fall as anticipated—particularly concerning given the report notes commentary about growing inflation risk—refinancing costs could be materially higher.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing £137.241m (£60.241m PWLB, £77m market) at 3.89%-4.65%; prior year £110.232m (£30.232m PWLB, £80m market); Bank of England base rate 3.75%; new borrowing weighted average 4.21%
findings.quote: The Council's strategy of borrowing on a short term basis will result in an increased refinancing risk in the near term.

findings.paper_title: May 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet - Final
findings.headline: Treasury management underspend of £3.0m is temporary and masks underlying directorate overspends of £7.6m
findings.detail: The council's net forecast overspend of £4.6m comprises directorate overspends of £7.6m offset by Central Services underspend of £3.0m from Treasury Management activity. The treasury benefit results from strategy to minimise borrowing and borrow short-term, combined with capital programme slippage in 2025/26 reducing financing needs. The council notes this 'will see the Council generate savings to support Council wide pressures' but acknowledges 'ongoing uncertainty in the global and UK economy remains an ongoing budget risk.'
findings.matters: The underlying service delivery position is materially worse than the reported £4.6m overspend, and the treasury benefit masking this is non-recurring, making the structural budget position weaker than headline figures suggest
findings.figures: Net overspend £4.6m, directorate overspends £7.6m, central services underspend £3.0m
findings.quote: Central Services has a £3.0m forecast underspend, reflecting savings from Treasury Management activity... This is an approach that will see the Council generate savings to support Council wide pressures.

findings.paper_title: May 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet - Final
findings.headline: Dinnington capital project budget increased by £1.263m (10.5% uplift) due to scope changes and post-acquisition cost pressures
findings.detail: The Dinnington regeneration project, approved at £12.049m in July 2024, now requires £13.312m. The budget increase reflects scope changes identified post-acquisition (demolition/rebuild instead of refurbishment: £735k), basement works (£145k), design enhancements (£206k), and construction inflation (£177k). A £805k contingency remains, but the council notes costs were only estimates when approved due to uncertainty about building conditions, with major changes only becoming clear after acquisition.
findings.matters: A 10.5% budget increase mid-project, largely driven by post-acquisition discoveries and scope changes, indicates estimation risk and the challenge of cost control on complex regeneration schemes
findings.figures: £12.049m approved budget (July 2024), £13.312m revised requirement, £1.263m increase (10.5%), scope change £735k, basements £145k, design £206k, inflation £177k
findings.quote: As the key acquisitions have taken place on the project, further refinements have been made to the construction costs and wider project costs. Along with this, there has been a change to the management of the construction side of the scheme and a scope change that will see one of the buildings demolished and rebuilt rather than refurbished as originally planned.

findings.matters: Growing placement numbers and shift toward higher-cost external residential care represents demand-led structural growth that may not be controllable, and the council acknowledges lack of clear mitigations to date

findings.paper_title: May 2026 Financial Monitoring to Cabinet - Final
findings.headline: DSG cumulative deficit projected to reach £19.9m by March 2028 when statutory override expires
findings.detail: The council forecasts an in-year DSG deficit of approximately £5.5m, with cumulative deficit of £8.4m by end of March 2027 rising to £19.9m by March 2028. When the statutory override ends in April 2028, the council will be required to address this cumulative deficit from its General Fund resources, creating a structural pressure. The High Needs Stability Grant is expected to cover 90% of deficits accumulated by March 2026, but future support beyond 2025/26 is not confirmed.
findings.matters: A £19.9m unfunded liability materialising in 2028 represents a substantial and structural pressure on the council's general fund that lenders would need to factor into their risk assessment
findings.figures: £5.5m in-year deficit, £8.4m cumulative by March 2027, £19.9m by March 2028, £10m annual ongoing impact projected
findings.quote: The projected position against DSG budgets and the removal of the statutory override from April 2028 will mean that the Council's DSG deficit will be £19.9m, which will rise year on year by around £10m a year based on current demand and inflationary projections.

findings.matters: A lender would want to understand delivery risk on these large regeneration projects—whether they are on track, delivering planned returns, and aligned with realistic market conditions, particularly for commercial developments like Markets and Wath.

findings.paper_title: Year End Outturn 2025-26 to Cabinet - July 2026
findings.headline: HRA underspend of £4.3m masks deferred maintenance; medium-term repair backlog flagged as growing
findings.detail: The HRA recorded a £4.3m underspend, allowing planned reserve use to be reduced from £7.2m to £2.9m. However, the report notes this helps 'mitigate financial challenges presented by increased maintenance requirements over the medium term'—suggesting the underspend may reflect deferred rather than cancelled work, and the true maintenance liability is growing.
findings.matters: HRA underspends driven by deferred maintenance accumulate long-term repair liabilities; reduced reserve drawdown suggests reserve adequacy is improving, but only if maintenance demand is truly stable—which the council's language suggests it is not.
findings.figures: £4.3m HRA underspend; planned reserve use reduced from £7.2m to £2.9m; HRA balance improved but future maintenance liability unclear
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account had an underspend of £4.3m. As a result of this the HRA use of reserves was able to be reduced from £7.2m to £2.9m. This will help the HRA to mitigate the financial challenges presented by increased maintenance requirements over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Year End Outturn 2025-26 to Cabinet - July 2026
findings.headline: Waste route optimisation saving only 60% delivered (£0.3m of £0.5m); full delivery now pushed to 2026/27
findings.detail: The council approved a £0.5m route optimisation saving for waste management in the 2025/26 budget. Only £0.3m was delivered, with the remaining £0.4m to be carried forward to 2026/27. The report states 'key actions have been completed' but provides no explanation for why the full saving could not be realised in-year.
findings.matters: Efficiency savings are among the few areas council budgets can directly control; missing 40% of an approved saving on waste indicates either over-optimistic initial planning or slippage in implementation. Carries forward the risk to a tighter 2026/27.
findings.figures: £0.3m delivered; £0.5m target; £0.4m shortfall carried to 2026/27
findings.quote: The Waste service did not fully deliver the £0.5m route optimisation saving approved as part of the Budget and Council Tax Report 2025/26. As work progresses on the route optimisation plan that will increase the efficiency of waste rounds, the position with regards to the delivery of this saving will become clearer.

findings.paper_title: Year End Outturn 2025-26 to Cabinet - July 2026
findings.headline: Markets service overspend (£0.5m) repeating pattern with no recovery plan as development continues
findings.detail: The Markets service had a £0.5m income shortfall in 2025/26, described as 'similar position to previous years' with an expectation this pattern will continue into 2026/27 as the markets complex development progresses. No restructuring, income recovery plan, or clear recovery trajectory is described.
findings.matters: A revenue service with a multi-year pattern of underperforming income, no documented recovery plan, and ongoing uncertainty from development activity represents a controllable but unmanaged financial weakness.
findings.figures: £0.5m Markets overspend; repeated across multiple years
findings.quote: The Markets service had a £0.5m overspend because of income shortfalls which is a similar position to previous years. This is likely to continue into next financial year as the development of the markets complex continues.

findings.paper_title: Year End Outturn 2025-26 to Cabinet - July 2026
findings.headline: Local Government Pay Award 3.2% (£2.3m unfunded) absorbs entire treasury management savings buffer
findings.detail: The 3.2% pay award cost £2.3m above budget allocation, entirely beyond the council's control. To absorb this plus inflationary pressures on energy, materials, and social care market prices, the council generated £7.6m in treasury management savings. This consumed the entire savings buffer, leaving zero headroom for external shocks in 2026/27 and beyond.
findings.matters: When uncontrollable costs (pay, inflation, market-driven care pricing) consume discretionary savings entirely, the council has no absorptive capacity for further external pressures; this signals tight financial headroom and vulnerability.
findings.figures: 3.2% pay award; £2.3m above budget; £7.6m treasury management savings generated to offset pressures
findings.quote: The Local Government Pay Award was agreed at 3.2% at all pay bands up to senior officer. The impact was £2.3m above the budget allocated when setting the Council's Budget. The Council has no control over the level of pay award agreed.

findings.paper_title: Year End Outturn 2025-26 to Cabinet - July 2026
findings.headline: Budget balance achieved through £3.1m last-minute improvements and savings delivery, not planned action
findings.detail: The December forecast predicted a £3.4m overspend to be funded from reserves. The final outturn was £0.3m, a £3.1m improvement achieved by services delivering 'further savings ahead of year-end, maximising grant allocations, improvements in income' and treasury management. While the end result is better, the fact that £3.1m of the correction came in the final quarter suggests weak mid-year forecasting and emergency budget-balancing rather than disciplined delivery.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial discipline through forecast accuracy and planned vs. reactive budget management; this council's trajectory shows deteriorating mid-year forecasts and increasing reliance on discretionary year-end actions to avoid reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £3.4m overspend forecast in December; £0.3m actual; £3.1m improvement in final quarter
findings.quote: The actual financial outturn position reflects an overspend of £0.3m, an improvement of £3.1m from the December Financial Monitoring reported to February Cabinet. This improvement was a result of service areas delivering further savings ahead of year-end, maximising grant allocations, improvements in income and the Council generating further savings in Treasury Management.

findings.paper_title: Year End Outturn 2025-26 to Cabinet - July 2026
findings.headline: Children's residential placements: 44 in external care against 24 budgeted; finance team flags as significant 2026/27 risk
findings.detail: Despite overall children in care numbers declining (475 vs 481), the council massively underestimated residential placement demand, placing 44 children externally against a budget for 24. Complexity of need is driving placement costs above inflation. The finance team has explicitly warned this pattern will persist into 2026/27 and requires tighter forecasting and mitigation action.
findings.matters: A £6.2m placement overspend that the council describes as a persistent 'significant financial risk' demonstrates inability to forecast or control this key cost driver; the acknowledgement of need for 'clearer actions to mitigate' suggests current mitigation is insufficient.
findings.figures: £6.2m underlying placement overspend; 44 external residential placements vs 24 budgeted; 475 children in care (down 6 from year start)
findings.quote: The year‑end placement numbers and underlying recurrent costs continue to present a significant financial risk for 2026/27. Work is underway to strengthen placement budget projections, alongside clearer actions to mitigate cost pressures.

findings.paper_title: Year End Outturn 2025-26 to Cabinet - July 2026
findings.headline: Mental health support cases rose 14% year-on-year against 1% system-wide growth, driving £7m Adult Social Care placement overspend
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspend was caused by rising demand and complexity of care packages, particularly for working-age adults with learning disabilities and mental health needs. Mental health support cases grew 14% year-on-year—nearly 14 times the 1% system-wide growth rate—driving care costs far above inflation. Staffing underspends only partially offset the placement cost overrun.
findings.matters: This indicates structural demand growth in ASC that the council cannot absorb through current budgets; the disproportionate mental health growth suggests either deteriorating community support outcomes or emerging population cohorts the council must plan for.
findings.figures: £7m underlying placement overspend; £5.9m directorate overspend; 14% rise in mental health support need cases
findings.quote: The main area of overspend was working age adults, especially people with learning disabilities and people with mental health need as packages increased significantly in the year in terms of demand and cost. There was a 14% rise in the number of people needing mental health support compared to 1% increase overall.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report and Actual Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: General Fund financing cost ratio improved from 12.24% to 10.11% of net revenue stream; HRA from 15.06% to 14.15%
findings.detail: The General Fund's financing costs (borrowing and related obligations, net of investment income) decreased from 12.24% of net revenue stream (original budget) to 10.11% (actual outturn). The HRA similarly improved from 15.06% to 14.15%. The improvement resulted from lower than expected additional borrowing and higher than forecast investment returns.
findings.matters: The council beat its financing cost budget due to a combination of lower than expected borrowing and higher investment returns. Peer finance directors need to understand whether this improvement is sustainable or relies on market conditions (lower rates) and capital underspending.
findings.figures: General Fund 12.24% (original budget) vs 10.11% (actual outturn); HRA 15.06% (original budget) vs 14.15% (actual outturn)
findings.quote: The General Fund ratio decreased from 12.24% (original budget) to 10.11% (actual out -turn). This was mainly as a result of reduced borrowing costs for the year as the Council undertook lower than expected additional borrowing during the year. The increased interest received on investments also contributed to this reduction.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report and Actual Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £25.7m reduces CFR and defers borrowing need into future years
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement at 31 March 2026 is £25.7m lower than the revised estimate approved at the mid-year review, due to slippage on multiple capital schemes and additional grant funding. This reduces the council's immediate borrowing need and generates savings on planned MRP and interest payments, but pushes these costs and the associated capital investment into future years.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage indicates the council did not deliver planned capital investment. Peers and lenders need to understand the underlying reasons and whether slippage will continue, as this affects the council's capital capacity and future borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: £25.7m CFR reduction; CFR at 31 March 2026 of £897.957m (excluding PFI and other long-term liabilities)
findings.quote: the closing CFR is £25.7m less than that approved in the revised indicator, via the Mid-Year report. The reduction is due to slippage on a number of capital schemes and additional grant funding gained

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report and Actual Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Net under-borrowing position increased to £347.128m while pursuing short-term borrowing strategy in anticipation of lower interest rates
findings.detail: The council's net under-borrowed position increased from £308.479m at 31 March 2025 to £347.128m at 31 March 2026. The council is pursuing a deliberate short-term borrowing strategy, taking only essential borrowing and planning refinancing in coming years, in anticipation of lower interest rates. All new borrowing in 2025/26 was short-term except £40m PWLB at 3.89% for 12 months.
findings.matters: A large and growing under-borrowed position indicates the council is making a conscious strategic bet on future interest rates. This creates significant refinancing risk if rates do not fall as anticipated, or if the council needs capital funding in a rising rate environment.
findings.figures: £347.128m net under-borrowed at 31 March 2026 (up from £308.479m); £142m new borrowing taken at weighted average 4.21%; £110.2m repaid at weighted average 4.89%
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Council continued to pursue its short-term borrowing strategy, supported by advice from its Treasury advisers. Borrowing is taken only as needed and will be refinanced in the next few years. This has resulted in an increase in the net under borrowed position.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report and Actual Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Treasury management savings of £7.6m used to support the council's 2025/26 overall outturn position
findings.detail: The council's treasury management underspend for 2025/26 is being used to support the overall outturn position. Treasury and capital financing decisions at year-end will enable further savings of in excess of £2.7m for 2026/27, though some of this is temporary due to capital programme slippage.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer finance directors need to understand whether the council is relying on non-recurring treasury gains to balance its budget. If these gains are temporary or dependent on capital slippage and lower interest rates, the underlying financial position may be weaker than headline outturn suggests.
findings.figures: £7.6m underspend 2025/26; £2.7m+ savings 2026/27 (some temporary)
findings.quote: a £7.6m underspend on the 2025/26 Treasury Management budget that has been used to support the Council's 2025/26 overall outturn position

findings.headline: Children's services overspent by £6.2m in 2025/26 despite reducing placements by 120+ since 2019/20, due to rising market prices

findings.headline: Council states 'future outlook remains challenging' for treasury management, despite recent savings from short-term borrowing strategy
findings.detail: The Council notes that its short-term borrowing approach has generated significant savings in recent years, essential to achieving balanced budgets, but explicitly assesses that future treasury prospects are uncertain and difficult.
findings.matters: A council's own assessment of future financial headwinds signals material pressure ahead and reduced financial flexibility.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The Council's approach to Treasury Management in recent years, utilising short term borrowing in particular, has generated significant savings for the Council, essential to achieving balanced budgets, but the future outlook remains challenging.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 Prudential Indicators and TM Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast to increase to £210.9m in 2026/27 from £168.4m in 2025/26; Council warns it must 'closely consider' prudential borrowing levels post-2026/27
findings.detail: The 26% increase in capital spending will require prudential borrowing of £99.1m in 2026/27, up from £68.8m in 2025/26. The Council explicitly states it will need to carefully evaluate prudential borrowing levels beyond 2026/27 to ensure overall debt remains manageable and sustainably financed, signalling concern about longer-term affordability at this scale.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender assessing sustainability must understand whether the expanded capital programme can be maintained without exceeding prudent debt limits.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure £210.906m (2026/27) vs £168.388m (2025/26); prudential borrowing requirement £99.114m (2026/27) vs £68.759m (2025/26)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 Prudential Indicators and TM Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Council borrowed £25m from South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority since mid-year report in November 2025; further borrowing expected before year-end

findings.matters: A lender and peer finance directors track councils' active refinancing and borrowing decisions to understand treasury management patterns and cash flow pressures.

This borrowing is to re-finance historic debt and support cash flow management.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Voluntary severance costs to take priority claim on capital receipts
findings.detail: The council will prioritise voluntary severance costs as the first claim on capital receipts generated in the year. This indicates planned staffing restructuring as part of the council's service transformation.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need to understand when councils are undertaking significant staffing reductions, as this affects both costs and service capability.
findings.figures: No amounts specified
findings.quote: the first call on capital receipts generated in the year will be utilised to meet the cost of voluntary severance

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Pay award pressures created £2.3m unbudgeted cost in 2025/26, with future pay award costs unfunded by government
findings.detail: The 2025/26 LGA Pay Award came in £2.3m worse than assumed in the budget. The council has now uplifted the MTFS by £1.7m per year to cover ongoing pay award exposure and the 6.75% Real Living Wage increase, but explicitly notes 'the Council has no control over these and Government do not provide additional funding to cover their impact.'
findings.matters: Pay award volatility is a structural risk the council cannot control or pass through to service users. The fact that government doesn't fund pay awards means every uplift must be absorbed through tax rises or service cuts.
findings.figures: £2.3m 2025/26 overspend from pay award; £1.7m annual MTFS uplift; Real Living Wage 6.75% to £13.45
findings.quote: Future pay awards remain a key area of uncertainty moving into 2026/27 as the Council has no control over these and Government do not provide additional funding to cover their impact.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Home to School Transport requires £0.5m additional p.a. investment despite policy tightening, reflecting national structural demand
findings.detail: The council has delivered policy changes and efficiency improvements but demand for Home to School Transport 'continues to rise', described as 'reflective of the national picture'. This requires sustained additional investment across the medium term (2026/27 to 2028/29).
findings.matters: This shows a service area where the council has limited control and demand is structural. It signals vulnerability to other national policy shifts that drive demand but don't come with funding.
findings.quote: Home to School Transport has seen continued increases in cost and demand in recent years and whilst the Council has delivered changes to the policy and improved transport efficiency to stem the cost increase, the demand continues to rise.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Speciality Steel, a major Business Rates payer, wound up with £4.2m debt write-off (Rotherham share £2.074m)
findings.detail: One of the council's biggest Business Rates payers entered financial difficulty in 2023/24 and is being wound up, requiring the council to write off accumulated Business Rates debt spanning from Q4 2023/24 through August 2025. This is material evidence of business base vulnerability.
findings.matters: Major employer/ratepayer collapse shows the council's tax base is not immune to significant economic shocks. The loss of one major payer creates both an immediate revenue hit and uncertainty about longer-term use of the site.
findings.figures: £4.2m total debt write-off; Rotherham £2,074,236.15; spanning 23/24-25/26
findings.quote: One of the Council's biggest Business Rates payers, Speciality Steel, is being wound up after entering financial difficulty during 2023/24. This presents a financial challenge to the Council through the need to write off £4.2m of Business Rates debt, spanning across Q4 2023/24 through to 21 August 2025.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: £9.3m funding gap forecast for 2028/29, emerging once the Fair Funding Review 2.0 windfall phases out
findings.detail: Although the council has achieved a balanced position for 2026/27 and 2027/28, this is heavily reliant on phased implementation of FFR 2.0 funding (33.3% per year over 3 years). The council explicitly flags a 'potential £9.3m funding gap in 2028/29', indicating that when the temporary funding boost exhausts, structural imbalance returns.
findings.matters: This signals that the council's current balance is temporary and dependent on external funding that phases out. A lender evaluating sustainability needs to understand the underlying structural gap that will re-emerge in three years.
findings.figures: £9.3m gap in 2028/29; FFR 2.0 phased at 33.3% per year over 2026/27-2028/29
findings.quote: Following the Council's technical MTFS updates, proposed budget decisions within this report, the impact of the FFR 2.0 and Provisional Financial Settlement, the Council has been able to propose a balanced budget for 2026/27 and 2027/28 with a potential £9.3m funding gap in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Forecast £3.4m overspend in 2025/26 with possible reserve drawdown, despite £5.4m Social Care Contingency already provisioned
findings.detail: The council's current-year (2025/26) financial monitoring shows a £9.2m directorate overspend, partially mitigated by a £5.4m contingency and Treasury Management savings, leaving a net £3.4m overspend. The council notes it 'is possible that even with mitigations the Council will need to call on Reserves to achieve a balanced outturn for 2025/26.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's current cash position and reserve depletion trajectory. Drawing reserves in the current year to cover overspends reduces resilience for future shocks and suggests the budget assumptions are not holding.
findings.figures: £3.4m forecast overspend; £9.2m directorate overspend; £5.4m Social Care Contingency
findings.quote: In order to help mitigate the position, Directors are expected to take all steps to reduce the overall overspend, ensuring grant maximisation, restricting any non-essential expenditure and delaying recruitment where possible.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Children's Social Care placements showing £5.7m overspend in current year with market costs rising faster than demand falls
findings.detail: The council carried out a 5-year benchmarking review and found that nationally children's social care placements have risen 52% (2019/20 to 2025/26) while Rotherham has only provided 29% inflation uplift. Market costs are rising faster than the council can control, and despite LAC numbers falling, the council explicitly describes placements as a 'budget risk'.
findings.matters: This shows a persistent structural cost pressure where the council's controls (reducing placements) are being overwhelmed by market-driven cost inflation. The £5.7m current-year overspend suggests this pressure is not yet solved.
findings.figures: £5.7m projected overspend 2025/26; £4.8m additional investment 2026/27; national inflation 52% vs council 29%
findings.quote: CYPS placements remains a budget risk with a projected overspend of £5.7m in 2025/26 due to rising market costs and challenges faced in delivering the in-house residential homes programme.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Adult Social Care explicitly identified as 'a significant long term financial risk' despite requiring £8.6m additional investment in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that Adult Social Care faces escalating cost pressures from rising complexity, ageing population, market inflation, and the 6.75% Real Living Wage increase. These are structural factors outside council control. The £8.6m injection addresses demand and market pressures but the council still flags this service as a persistent financial risk within its Medium Term Financial Strategy.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether social care pressures will stabilize or continue to erode the council's financial position. The explicit 'long term financial risk' flag suggests the council expects ongoing demands on its budget.
findings.figures: £8.6m additional investment in 2026/27; Real Living Wage increase 6.75% to £13.45
findings.quote: Considering the pressures within Adult Social Care demand, this service still represents a significant long term financial risk within the Council's Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet report - HRA Business Plan Rent Setting and Service Charges 2026-27 (002) (003) JE cr amends
findings.headline: HRA has historically subsidised district heating by £850k (2023/24–2025/26) to keep tenant costs down; 2026/27 proposes surplus model instead
findings.detail: The council maintained district heating unit rates to match average Ofgem gas bills using HRA subsidy (approx £850k over three years). From 2026/27, the plan switches to a 13.09p/kWh rate (matching April–June 2025 Ofgem cap) which is forecast to generate a £150k surplus instead, used to offset the historic deficit. This is a reversal of subsidy direction but creates exposure if energy prices fall faster than Ofgem cap.
findings.matters: District heating is a ring-fenced service that has required ongoing HRA funding. The switch to surplus model assumes energy price stability; if Ofgem caps fall unexpectedly, the council may face pressure to re-subsidise to maintain tenant affordability.
findings.figures: £850k HRA subsidy 2023/24–2025/26; £150k forecast 2026/27 surplus; unit rate 13.09p per kWh; average annual cost £834 (£60 below average Ofgem gas bill).
findings.quote: In prior years to maintain lower district heating costs the HRA has subsidised the cost of the heat network by approximately £850k between 2023/24 to 2025/26. Any surplus generated in 2026/27 will go towards netting off this deficit while ensuring tenants on the district heating network continue to pay a fair price in line with the average gas bill under Ofgem price cap.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet report - HRA Business Plan Rent Setting and Service Charges 2026-27 (002) (003) JE cr amends
findings.headline: Capital borrowing of £124m planned for housing investment in years 3-10, rising to £165m if convergence is not approved
findings.detail: The Plan assumes borrowing at discounted PWLB rates for HRA investment in existing stock and housing delivery. Additional borrowing rises to £165m if convergence is unavailable, with repayment of non-growth borrowing delayed from years 11-14 to years 14-28. Interest cover ratios shown in Appendix 10 indicate manageable debt servicing.
findings.matters: HRA borrowing is secured against rental income. An increase to £165m (34% higher) without convergence would extend debt life and reduce flexibility. A lender needs to track this conditional borrowing.
findings.figures: £124m borrowing years 3-10 under Option 3 (with convergence); £165m if Option 1 (no convergence); repayment of non-growth borrowing years 11-14 (Option 3) or years 14-28 (Option 1).
findings.quote: The Plan makes provision for additional borrowing of £124m in years 3 to 10 of the plan to fund the additional investment in existing stock and the on-going Housing Delivery Programme. Subject to the rent convergence announcement, if option 1 is implemented the borrowing requirement rises to £165m with repayment of loans not for housing growth not possible until years 14-28.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet report - HRA Business Plan Rent Setting and Service Charges 2026-27 (002) (003) JE cr amends
findings.headline: Net zero commitments estimated at £600m — acknowledged as 'formidable challenge' with no long-term funding strategy identified
findings.detail: To meet the council's 2040 net zero target (10 years ahead of UK 2050), the HRA will need to invest approximately £600m over the 30-year plan. The paper notes this 'becomes even more significant' in drawing external funding and references participation in national grant schemes but does not specify sources, amounts, or contingency if grants do not materialise.
findings.matters: Net zero retrofit is a long-duration, high-risk capital programme. Overruns are common in retrofit projects. A £600m cost estimate without identified funding mechanisms represents material downside risk to the HRA's long-term financial position.
findings.figures: Circa £600m estimated cost for net zero by 2040; £41m + £18m allocated in current plan (£59m total, leaving £541m unbudgeted).
findings.quote: Initial estimates put the cost of this at circa £600m which represents a formidable challenge to the HRA. As a result, this means that drawing in external funding to progress net zero commitments becomes even more significant.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet report - HRA Business Plan Rent Setting and Service Charges 2026-27 (002) (003) JE cr amends
findings.headline: Multiple regulatory compliance costs emerging with no budget allocation — particularly Decent Homes 2 and new hazard standards
findings.detail: Council states explicitly: 'The 2026/27 HRA Business plan does not currently include any assumptions regarding Decent Homes 2 or the minimum energy efficiency standards as the associated costs are unknown currently.' New rules include Awaab's Law phases 2-3 (electrical, fire, structural, excess cold/heat), Competence and Conduct Standard (October 2026), Heat Network Regulations (Ofgem oversight), and proposed Decent Homes 2 with EPC Band C by 2030 and damp-specific criteria.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted regulatory requirements are a common source of HRA cost overruns and borrowing surprises. The paper shows awareness but no provision, meaning costs will either hit unexpectedly or programmes will be delayed.
findings.figures: £41m allocated for EPC Band C for 9,300 properties; £18m Warm Homes grant for c.1,000 properties; unspecified costs for Awaab's Law phases 2-3, Competence/Conduct Standard, Decent Homes 2.
findings.quote: The 2026/27 HRA Business plan does not currently include any assumptions regarding Decent Homes 2 or the minimum energy efficiency standards as the associated costs are unknown currently.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet report - HRA Business Plan Rent Setting and Service Charges 2026-27 (002) (003) JE cr amends
findings.headline: Repairs and complaint handling remain weak areas despite 28% reduction in complaints and £2.9m budget increase to £30.5m
findings.detail: Recent Tenant Satisfaction Measures identified 'issues in repairs delays, poor quality, damp/mould, Anti-Social Behaviour (ASB) response gaps and weak communication'. A 28% reduction in complaints occurred in 2024/25, but repairs remains a weak area. The council is increasing repairs/maintenance revenue by £2.9m to £30.5m (to £6.5m responsive, £6.7m planned, £2.8m damp/mould), suggesting the problem is not new money but delivery.
findings.matters: Persistent failures after budget increases indicate either operational dysfunction or demand exceeding capacity even with additional spend. This signals delivery risk on the £41m thermal efficiency and £43.3m existing-homes capital programmes.
findings.figures: 2024/25 complaints down 28%; responsive repairs budget £6.5m; planned repairs £6.7m; damp/mould £2.8m; total repairs/maintenance revenue increase £2.9m.
findings.quote: There are however persistent issues in repairs, timeliness, and complaint handling. This is backed up by recent TSMs that identified issues in repairs delays, poor quality, damp/mould, Anti-Social Behaviour (ASB) response gaps and weak communication.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet report - HRA Business Plan Rent Setting and Service Charges 2026-27 (002) (003) JE cr amends
findings.headline: HRA reserves being drawn down by £11m (58%) in 2026-27 to fund capital investment
findings.detail: General HRA revenue reserve forecast to fall from £19.348m (31 March 2026) to £8.29m (31 March 2027). This £11.058m transfer funds £13.8m of capital expenditure; only £2.7m comes from operational surplus. Reserves stay above the stated minimum of £5.5m but offer limited headroom for unexpected cost pressures.
findings.matters: A rapid reserve depletion signals the council is consuming equity to fund growth. If capital costs overrun or income disappoints, the buffer evaporates quickly, forcing rent increases or borrowed contingency.
findings.figures: Reserve reduction of £11.058m; minimum required balance £5.5m (uplifted by CPI annually); revenue contribution to capital £13.836m.
findings.quote: Budget proposals for 2026/27 would see the reserve reduced to £8.3m by 31 March 2027. This is within the parameters of the minimum HRA revenue balance.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet report - HRA Business Plan Rent Setting and Service Charges 2026-27 (002) (003) JE cr amends
findings.headline: HRA financial viability depends entirely on a Government rent convergence announcement due January 2026
findings.detail: The council's recommended Business Plan (Option 3) assumes rent convergence of up to £2 per week is available. If Government does not announce this, rents would increase only by 4.8% (CPI+1%), forcing reversion to Option 1 which leaves HRA reserves at minimum balance for years 2-5 onwards. The council states explicitly that without convergence, the plan 'does not provide financial resilience'.
findings.matters: A lender needs certainty over cash flow. This plan has a single point of failure in a Government policy decision outside the council's control, with a four-month lag before the decision lands.
findings.figures: Option 3 (with convergence) generates £83m additional rental income over 30 years. Without it, reserves drop to minimum £5.5m for extended periods, eliminating buffer for cost shocks.
findings.quote: Without the convergence announcement the proposed rent increase would revert to the current rent settlement level of CPI+1%, which is option 1. This would result in the revenue balances being at minimum balance for years 2-5 and further years throughout the plan which does not provide financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: Mid-Year Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators Monitoring Report - 2025-25
findings.headline: Council holds £69.4m investments entirely in AAA-rated money market funds; no direct lending to banks or local authorities.
findings.detail: The council's £69.4m of investments at 30 September 2025 are entirely deployed in AAA-rated Money Market Funds yielding 3.98-4.04%. No funds are placed directly with banks or other local authorities. The council describes this positioning as reflecting 'heightened' counterparty risk concerns in the current market environment, where the primary investment objective is safeguarding principal repayment rather than maximising yield. The council achieved a return of 4.25% against a SONIA benchmark of 4.19%, outperforming by 6 basis points.
findings.matters: This shows how a council is managing treasury counterparty risk in the current environment. The move entirely to AAA-rated MMFs and away from direct local authority lending reflects a deliberate reduction in direct credit exposure. A peer council watching treasury management or a lender assessing risk management practices would note this as a conservative positioning.
findings.figures: Total investments at 30/09/25: £69.4m; allocation to Money Market Funds: £69.4m (100%); allocation to banks: £0m; allocation to local authorities: £0m; MMF yields: 3.98-4.04%; actual return achieved: 4.25% vs SONIA 4.19%
findings.quote: As a result of these underlying market concerns, officers continue to implement an operational investment strategy which maintains the tight controls already in place in the approved Investment Strategy.

findings.paper_title: Mid-Year Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators Monitoring Report - 2025-25
findings.headline: Borrowing in 40+ year maturity tranches totals £289m (41% of actual borrowing); council notes increased repricing risk on LOBO rate-reset calls.
findings.detail: The council's maturity structure includes £249m of borrowing with next repayment or LOBO call dates in the 40-50 year window (35.62% of total borrowing) and £40m in the 50+ year window (5.72%). The council notes that given interest rates have risen since these loans were issued, lenders are more likely to exercise LOBO rate-reset options. When a lender exercises this option, the council can choose to repay at par or accept a new rate. The council states: 'Given the significant increase in interest rates some of these loans have rates below the prevailing lending rates. There is therefore an increased chance that a lender will increase the loan rate at which point the Council has the option to pay the higher rate or repay the loan.' No LOBO calls were reported during the first six months of 2025/26.
findings.matters: A lender or peer council needs to understand the council's exposure to refinancing events. If LOBO loans are called and repaid at par, the council must replace that funding, likely at current higher long-term rates, materially increasing debt service costs. £289m is material (41% of actual borrowing at mid-year). This represents a real economic event requiring cash and funding replacement, not merely a 'repricing' of existing debt.
findings.figures: 40-50 year maturity tranche: £249m (35.62% of borrowing); 50+ year tranche: £40m (5.72%); Combined £289m of £698.1m actual borrowing at 30/09/25
findings.quote: Given the significant increase in interest rates some of these loans have rates below the prevailing lending rates. There is therefore an increased chance that a lender will increase the loan rate at which point the Council has the option to pay the higher rate or repay the loan.

findings.paper_title: Mid-Year Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators Monitoring Report - 2025-25
findings.headline: Bank of England base rate has fallen from 4.5% to 4.0% with further cuts expected; long-term borrowing rates remain elevated at 5.97% for 50-year PWLB.
findings.detail: During the first half of 2025/26, the Bank of England base rate dropped from 4.5% to 4.0% and further cuts are expected. Short-term borrowing costs have fallen accordingly, with 6-month PWLB rates now around 4.5% (down from 5% a year earlier). However, longer-term borrowing rates remain elevated: 50-year PWLB loans have ranged from lows of 5.45% to highs of 6.12%, currently standing at 5.97%. This is higher than the previous year. The council continues to monitor rates and retains discretion to borrow if rates prove favourable.
findings.matters: The council's entire short-term borrowing strategy rests on the assumption that longer-term rates will fall in future. If long-term rates remain elevated or rise further, the council would face the choice of accepting higher borrowing costs (ending the savings), continuing to roll over expensive short-term debt, or reducing its capital programme. The PWLB also offers a discounted rate for HRA borrowing until March 2026, which the council notes as a possible opportunity but has not committed to.
findings.figures: Base rate: fell from 4.5% (April 2025) to 4.0% (September 2025); 50-year PWLB: highs 6.12%, lows 5.45%, current 5.97%; 6-month PWLB: approximately 4.5% (Sept 2025) vs 5.0% (Sept 2024)
findings.quote: The Bank of England has started to cut Base Rate and the cost of short term borrowing has reduced as a result, with further reductions expected in the near future. The costs for longer term borrowing however remain high reflecting the yield on UK gilts.

findings.paper_title: Mid-Year Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators Monitoring Report - 2025-25
findings.headline: Treasury management strategy forecasting £3.4m savings against £3m budget, described by council as essential to achieving balanced budgets.
findings.detail: The council's treasury budget for 2025/26 built in a £3m saving, with current forecasts showing an additional £3.4m savings will be realised, totalling £6.4m. This comes from the under-borrowing and short-term borrowing strategy, which maintains an interest rate differential of 1.58% between short-term borrowing costs and long-term rates. If the council were fully borrowed, this differential would cost £5.008m per year. The council explicitly states: 'The Council's approach to Treasury Management in recent years, utilising short term borrowing in particular, has generated significant savings for the Council, essential to achieving balanced budgets'.
findings.matters: This reveals material budget dependency: the council's stated ability to balance its budget relies on continuing to realise these treasury savings through the gap between short and long-term rates. If that gap closes, or long-term rates fall sharply, forcing the council to borrow long-term to lock in lower rates, the savings would be at risk and the council would face budget pressure.
findings.figures: Treasury budget saving target: £3m; current forecast additional saving: £3.4m; annual cost of being fully borrowed at current differentials: £5.008m (under-borrowing and short-term borrowing × 1.58%)
findings.quote: The Council's approach to Treasury Management in recent years, utilising short term borrowing in particular, has generated significant savings for the Council, essential to achieving balanced budgets, but the future outlook remains challenging.

findings.paper_title: Mid-Year Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators Monitoring Report - 2025-25
findings.headline: Council's end-of-year borrowing strategy revised to hold £191.3m under-borrowing and £125m short-term borrowing, against original plan of £27.6m under-borrowing and £0m short-term.
findings.detail: The council's borrowing position at mid-year shows a significant strategic shift from the original plan. The original estimate projected the council would be £27.6m under-borrowed by year-end with no short-term borrowing. The revised estimate now plans £191.3m under-borrowing and £125m short-term borrowing by year-end. At 30 September 2025, the council is £325.7m under-borrowed (vs original estimate of £47.6m at that date), having borrowed £57m to date and holding £69.4m in investments. The council plans £65m additional borrowing before year-end, all on a short-term basis.
findings.matters: This reveals a deliberate strategic shift: moving from a plan to be substantially long-term borrowed by year-end to a plan to maintain significant short-term borrowing exposure. For a lender, it signals the council's reliance on the short-term debt market for refinancing. For a peer council, it shows the calculated trade-off between immediate interest savings (around 1.58% differential) and rollover risk on £125m of short-term debt.
findings.figures: Revised position year-end 31/03/26: Under-borrowing £191.3m (vs £27.6m original); Short-term borrowing £125m (vs £0m original); Mid-year position 30/09/25: Under-borrowing £325.7m; Planned additional borrowing Oct-Mar 2026: £65m
findings.quote: The current strategy is to delay all new borrowing as late as possible and to only enter into short term borrowing in order to minimise the interest cost to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Audit Findings (ISA260) Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: Unadjusted audit findings: £7.1m in misstatements management chose not to correct
findings.detail: Auditors identified three misstatements totalling £7.1m impact to the deficit which management decided not to adjust for in the published accounts. This includes a £1.1m understatement of fees and charges income. These remain uncorrected despite being material to many users.
findings.matters: Management's decision not to correct identified misstatements below materiality threshold (£15.2m) suggests either tight reserves or deliberate position-taking on close calls.
findings.figures: £7.1m total misstatements unadjusted; £1.1m fees and charges income understatement
findings.quote: We identified three misstatements that management have decided not to adjust for in the financial statements presented for approval, one of which only impacts on disclosures in the notes to the financial statements. These misstatements would result in a £7.1m adjustment to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement as a reduction to the deficit outturn and would increase usable reserves by £1.1m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Audit Findings (ISA260) Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: School conversions to academies: £20m+ reduction in land and buildings asset base
findings.detail: Over £20m of the £30m fall in other land and buildings value resulted from four schools converting to academies during the financial year, removing them from the Council's asset base and reducing access to their use.
findings.matters: Academy conversions reduce the Council's asset base and future income-generating potential; lenders need to track whether this trend continues and impacts borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £20m+ from four school conversions out of £30m total reduction
findings.quote: The draft accounts indicated a fall in the carrying value of other land and buildings totalling £30m, of this over £20m is the result of four schools converting to academies during the financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Audit Findings (ISA260) Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: £13m audit adjustment required to newly-acquired council dwellings after valuation error
findings.detail: The Council acquired £23m of residential properties during the year as part of its housing stock expansion programme, but initially recorded them at historic cost. Auditors identified they should be valued at social housing (EUV-SH) rates, requiring a £13m downward adjustment. This suggests a control gap in capital asset accounting.
findings.matters: A £13m valuation miss on recent acquisitions indicates either weak controls over asset classification or insufficient challenge of purchase valuations on capital schemes.
findings.figures: £23m acquisition, £13m downward adjustment to comply with Code requirements
findings.quote: The Council acquired residential properties totalling £23m during the year as part of its programme to build out its housing stock. These were recorded at historic cost in the draft accounts... resulting in a fall in the carrying value totalling £13m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Audit Findings (ISA260) Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: Riverside House office accommodation: £5m asset impairment due to weak market demand
findings.detail: The most significant individual revaluation movement was Riverside House, which showed a £5m fall in carrying value on an existing use basis. The auditor's report attributes this to 'perceived weaker demand for office accommodation', suggesting structural demand weakness for the Council's office assets.
findings.matters: Office real estate demand is declining post-pandemic; this is a specific indicator that the Council holds office assets at risk of further impairment.

findings.quote: The most significant individual valuation movement related to Riverside House, which showed a fall of £5m on an existing use basis reflecting perceived weaker demand for office accommodation.

news_drafts.headline: Rotherham forecasts £8.1m schools-grant deficit for 2026/27 as its SEND reform plan is approved
news_drafts.lead:
Rotherham Council's Cabinet was told that the in-year deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, is forecast at £8.1m for 2026/27, which is £1.7m worse than the position reported in July. Of the total, £7.7m is in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, and £0.4m is in early years. The September financial monitoring paper attributes the increase to higher than expected demand for special school and Independent Specialist Provider placements for pupils with education, health and care plans. No maintained schools are reporting a forecast deficit for the year.

The cumulative deficit is forecast at £10.4m by 31 March 2027 and £20.4m by March 2028, when the statutory override, a government rule that keeps such deficits off the council's main accounts, ends. The paper says it could then rise by around £10m a year. If the High Needs Stability Grant continues to cover 90% of eligible deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, the remaining liability at March 2028 would be around £4m, to be funded from reserves. The medium-term financial strategy paper calls that continued grant the council's best estimate and "not a guaranteed position".

The council's Local SEND Reform Plan, approved by the Department for Education on 2 October 2026, projects high needs spending of £80.5m in 2028/29 and £85.5m in 2030/31 without reform. With successful delivery, the figures are £78m and £78.1m. The plan states a cumulative deficit of over £68.9m by 2030/31 without reform. The council has been allocated £2.2m for 2026/27 for the Experts at Hand model in schools, and a £3.4m high needs capital allocation.
